problems.title: Reactions of copper and its compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (National Exam Part II).

This question involves several reactions of copper and its compounds.

a. A sample of copper metal is dissolved in $6\,\mathrm{M}$ nitric acid contained in a round bottom flask. This reaction yields a blue solution and emits a colorless gas which is found to be nitric oxide. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.

b. The water is evaporated from the blue solution to leave a blue solid. When the blue solid is heated further, a second reaction occurs. This reaction produces a mixture of nitrogen dioxide gas, oxygen gas and a black oxide of copper.

i. A sample of the dried gas, collected in a $125\,\mathrm{mL}$ flask at $35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $725\,\mathrm{mm\ Hg}$, weighed $0.205\,\mathrm{g}$. Find the average molar mass of the gas and the molar $\ce{NO2}/\ce{O2}$ ratio in it.

ii. These data were obtained for the black solid;

$$\begin{array}{lr}
\text{Mass of empty flask:} & 39.49\ \mathrm{g} \\
\text{Mass of flask + copper metal:} & 40.86\ \mathrm{g} \\
\text{Mass of flask + oxide of copper:} & 41.21\ \mathrm{g}
\end{array}$$

Determine the formula of the oxide of copper.

c. If some of the blue solution were lost due to splattering during the evaporation, what would be the effect on the calculated percentage of copper in the black oxide? Explain.

d. If all of the blue solid were not decomposed into the black oxide during the final heating, what would be the effect on the calculated percentage of copper in the oxide? Explain.

problems.title: Hydrazine as rocket propellant: enthalpy changes
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (National Exam Part II).

Liquid hydrazine, $\ce{N2H4}$, is sometimes used as a rocket propellant.

a. Write an equation for the formation of hydrazine from its elements and use the combustion equations below to derive an equation in which $\Delta H_\mathrm{f}^\circ$ for liquid hydrazine is expressed in terms of $\Delta H_1$, $\Delta H_2$ and $\Delta H_3$.

$$\ce{1/2 N2(g) + O2(g) -> NO2(g)} \qquad \Delta H_1$$

$$\ce{H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> H2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H_2$$

$$\ce{N2H4(l) + 3O2(g) -> 2NO2(g) + 2H2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H_3$$

b. In a rocket, liquid hydrazine is reacted with liquid hydrogen peroxide to produce nitrogen and water vapor. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.

c. Calculate $\Delta H_\mathrm{rxn}^\circ$ for the reaction represented in 2b.

$$\begin{array}{|lr|}
\hline
 & \Delta H_\mathrm{f}^\circ\ \ \mathrm{kJ/mol} \\
\hline
\ce{N2H4(l)} & 50.6 \\
\ce{H2O2(l)} & -187.8 \\
\ce{H2O(g)} & -285.8 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

d. Calculate $\Delta H_\mathrm{rxn}^\circ$ for the reaction in 2b using bond dissociation energies.

$$\begin{array}{|lr|lr|}
\hline
\text{Bond} & \text{Dissociation Energy, kJ/mol} & \text{Bond} & \text{Dissociation Energy, kJ/mol} \\
\hline
\ce{N-N} & 167 & \ce{O-O} & 142 \\
\ce{N=N} & 418 & \ce{O=O} & 494 \\
\ce{N#N} & 942 & \ce{O-H} & 459 \\
\ce{N-H} & 386 & & \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

e. Which value of $\Delta H_\mathrm{rxn}^\circ$ (that calculated in part c or part d) is likely to be more accurate? Justify your answer.

f. Calculate the maximum temperature of the combustion gases if all the energy generated in the reaction goes into raising the temperature of those gases. [The heat capacities of $\ce{N2(g)}$ and $\ce{H2O(g)}$ are $29.1\,\mathrm{J/(mol{\cdot}^\circ C)}$ and $33.6\,\mathrm{J/(mol{\cdot}^\circ C)}$, respectively.]

You may assume the solution's specific heat capacity is $4.025\,\mathrm{J\cdot g^{-1}\cdot{}^\circ C^{-1}}$ and the enthalpy of neutralization is $-55.9\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per mole of $\ce{H2O}$.

c. When $0.221\,\mathrm{g}$ of magnesium turnings are added to $49.9\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $1.01\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ and $49.7\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{H2O}$ in the same calorimeter, the temperature increases by $9.67\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Write a balanced equation for the reaction that occurs and calculate the $\Delta H$ per mole of magnesium. (Assume the solution's specific heat capacity is $3.862\,\mathrm{J\cdot g^{-1}\cdot{}^\circ C^{-1}}$ and the calorimeter constant is the value obtained in b.)

d. When $0.576\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{MgO}$ react with $51.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $1.01\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ and $50.1\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{H2O}$ in the same calorimeter the temperature rises $4.72\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Write a balanced equation for this reaction and calculate its $\Delta H$ per mole of $\ce{MgO}$ using the same assumptions as in part c.

problems.title: Kinetics of the bromate-bromide reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (National Exam Part II).

The reaction of bromate and bromide ions in acid solution is represented by the equation,

$$\ce{5 Br-(aq) + BrO3-(aq) + 6 H3O+(aq) -> 3 Br2(aq) + 9 H2O(l)}$$

In order to measure the rate of the reaction, stock solutions were prepared as shown in the table:

Stock Solution Concentrations

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline
\text{Stock } \ce{Br-} \text{ solution} & 1.37\,\mathrm{M} \\
\hline
\text{Stock } \ce{BrO3-} \text{ solution} & 7.10\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M} \\
\hline
\text{Stock } \ce{H3O+} \text{ solution} & 0.573\,\mathrm{M} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

Reaction mixtures were prepared by mixing the volumes of solutions listed below, and the initial rate of disappearance of bromate ion was measured.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Expt.} & \text{Vol. } \ce{Br-} \text{ stock (mL)} & \text{Vol. } \ce{BrO3-} \text{ stock (mL)} & \text{Vol } \ce{H3O+} \text{ stock (mL)} & \text{Vol } \ce{H2O} \text{ (mL)} & \text{Initial rate of } \ce{BrO3-} \text{ disappearance } (\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}\cdot s^{-1}}) \\
\hline
1 & 0.100 & 0.500 & 1.000 & 1.400 & 5.63\times10^{-6} \\
\hline
2 & 0.200 & 0.500 & 1.000 & 1.300 & 1.09\times10^{-5} \\
\hline
3 & 0.100 & 1.000 & 1.000 & 0.900 & 1.13\times10^{-5} \\
\hline
4 & 0.200 & 0.500 & 0.700 & 1.600 & 5.50\times10^{-6} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Calculate the rate of appearance of $\ce{Br2(aq)}$ in experiment one.

b. Write the rate law for this reaction and give the value of the specific rate constant, $k$.

c. The following mechanism is proposed for the reaction:

$$\begin{array}{ll}
\text{(I)} & \ce{BrO3-(aq) + H3O+(aq) -> HBrO3(aq) + H2O(l)} \\
\text{(II)} & \ce{HBrO3(aq) + H3O+(aq) -> H2BrO3+(aq) + H2O(l)} \\
\text{(III)} & \ce{H2BrO3+(aq) -> BrO2+(aq) + H2O(l)} \\
\text{(IV)} & \ce{BrO2+(aq) + Br-(aq) -> BrOBrO(aq)} \\
\text{(V)} & \ce{BrOBrO(aq) + Br-(aq) -> Br2(aq) + BrO2-(aq)} \\
 & \text{Subsequent reactions of } \ce{BrO2-(aq)} \text{ are fast.}
\end{array}$$

i. Draw a Lewis structure of $\ce{BrO2+}$ and predict its geometry.

ii. Given the rate law you determined in b, which of the steps (I)-(V) could potentially be rate-limiting? Justify your answer.

Problem 1 (National Exam Part II).

$5.60\,\mathrm{g}$ of solid carbon is placed in a rigid evacuated $2.5\,\mathrm{L}$ container. Carbon dioxide is added to the container to a final pressure of $1.50\,\mathrm{atm}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

a. Calculate the number of moles of each reactant in the container originally.

b. The container is heated to $1100\,\mathrm{K}$ and the following reaction occurs: $\ce{C(s) + CO2(g) <=> 2 CO(g)}$ $\Delta H^\circ = 173\,\mathrm{kJ}$

i. Calculate the pressure in the container at this temperature before the reaction takes place.

ii. When equilibrium is reached the pressure inside the container is $1.75$ times that calculated in b.i. Determine the equilibrium partial pressures of $\ce{CO2(g)}$ and $\ce{CO(g)}$.

iii. Write the equilibrium expression for this reaction, $K_\mathrm{p}$.

iv. Calculate the value of $K_\mathrm{p}$ for this reaction at $1100\,\mathrm{K}$.

c. Predict the effect on the number of moles of carbon monoxide of each of the following changes made to this system at equilibrium. Give reasons for your predictions.

i. The volume of the container is increased to $5.0\,\mathrm{L}$.

ii. The pressure inside the container is increased by adding helium.

iii. The temperature of the system is increased to $1200\,\mathrm{K}$.

iv. The amount of solid carbon is increased to $6.00\,\mathrm{g}$.

problems.title: Thermodynamics and energetics of photosynthesis
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (National Exam Part II).

Green plants utilize sunlight to convert $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ to glucose ($\ce{C6H12O6}$) and $\ce{O2}$.

a. Write a balanced equation for this process.

b. Use the information in the accompanying table to calculate

i. $\Delta H^\circ$

ii. $\Delta S^\circ$

iii. $\Delta G^\circ$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ for this reaction.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Substance} & \Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{f}\ \ \mathrm{kJ/mol} & S^\circ\ \ \mathrm{J/mol{\cdot}K} \\
\hline
\ce{CO2(g)} & -393.5 & 213.2 \\
\hline
\ce{H2O(l)} & -285.8 & 69.9 \\
\hline
\ce{C6H12O6(s)} & -1273.3 & 212.1 \\
\hline
\ce{O2(g)} & & 205.0 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

c. Comment on the spontaneity of this reaction at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and other temperatures.

d. Green plants use light with wavelengths near $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ for this process. Calculate

i. the energy of a $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ photon,

ii. $\Delta G^\circ$ for the formation of one molecule of glucose by the reaction in 2a,

iii. the minimum number of $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ photons required to make one molecule of glucose by the reaction in 2a.

e. All of the photosynthesis on earth in a year stores $3.4 \times 10^{18}\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of solar energy.

i. Use the $\Delta G^\circ$ for the photosynthetic reaction to calculate the number of moles of $\ce{CO2}$ removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis each year.

ii. Determine the mass of carbon that is fixed annually by photosynthesis.

problems.title: Vanadium oxidation states and redox titration

a. Calculate the number of moles of vanadium dissolved and the molarity of vanadium ions in this solution.

b. Write the electron configuration of a neutral gaseous vanadium atom.

c. Give the oxidation state of vanadium in the yellow solution and outline your reasoning.

d. A $25.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ portion of this yellow solution is reduced with excess zinc amalgam under an inert atmosphere to give a violet solution. A $10.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot of this violet solution is titrated with a solution of $2.23 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KMnO4}$ in acid forming $\ce{Mn^2+}$. A volume of $13.20\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the $\ce{MnO4^-}$ solution is required to convert the vanadium back to yellow. Determine the:

i. number of moles of $\ce{MnO4^-}$ used in this titration,

ii. mole ratio of vanadium ions to $\ce{MnO4^-}$ ions in this titration,

iii. oxidation number change for vanadium in this titration and the oxidation state of vanadium ions in the violet solution.

e. When $2.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the violet solution are mixed with $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the original yellow solution, a green solution results. When this ratio is reversed a bright blue solution is formed. Determine the oxidation states of the green and blue vanadium ions. Support your answers with calculations.

problems.title: Kinetics of the reaction of NO with ozone
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (National Exam Part II).

The reaction $\ce{NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g)}$ is first order in each reactant with an activation energy, $E_\mathrm{a}$, of $11.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ and a rate constant of $k = 1.2 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

a. Calculate the value of the pre-exponential factor, $A$, in the equation $k = Ae^{-E_\mathrm{a}/RT}$.

b. Would the $A$ factor for the chemical reaction $\ce{NO(g) + N2O(g) -> NO2(g) + N2(g)}$ be expected to be larger or smaller than the $A$ factor in the above reaction if each reaction occurs in a single step? Outline your reasoning.

c. Calculate the rate constant for this reaction at $75\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

d. The following two-step mechanism has been proposed for this reaction:

$$\ce{O3(g) -> O2(g) + O(g)} \qquad \text{Step 1}$$

$$\ce{NO(g) + O(g) -> NO2(g)} \qquad \text{Step 2}$$

State and explain whether this mechanism is consistent with the observed rate law.

Account for the following observations on the basis of electrochemical principles. The Standard Reduction Potentials are provided.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline
\ce{2 HOCl(aq) + 2 H+(aq) + 2 e^- -> Cl2(g) + 2 H2O(l)} & E^\circ = 1.61\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{Cl2(g) + 2 e^- -> 2 Cl^-(aq)} & E^\circ = 1.36\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{O2(g) + 4 H+(aq) + 2 e^- -> 2 H2O(l)} & E^\circ = 1.23\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{Cu^2+(aq) + 2 e^- -> Cu(s)} & E^\circ = 0.34\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{Sn^2+(aq) + 2 e^- -> Sn(s)} & E^\circ = -0.14\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{Fe^2+(aq) + 2 e^- -> Fe(s)} & E^\circ = -0.44\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{Zn^2+(aq) + 2 e^- -> Zn(s)} & E^\circ = -0.76\,\mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. In a voltaic cell made with Cu metal in a $1.0\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{CuSO4}$ and Zn metal in $1.0\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{ZnSO4}$ the Zn is the anode and the cell potential is more than $1.0\,\mathrm{V}$. When aqueous sodium sulfide is added to the $\ce{CuSO4}$ solution the cell potential decreases substantially.

b. Iron metal corrodes readily in moist air but this corrosion can be prevented when iron is coated with tin or zinc. Corrosion is prevented when the zinc coating is intact or broken. In contrast, corrosion is prevented by coating iron with tin only as long as the tin coating remains intact but actually occurs faster when there is a break in the tin coating.

c. In acid solution chloride and hypochlorite ions react to form chlorine gas whereas in basic solution chlorine gas reacts to form chloride and hypochlorite ions.

\hline

\hline

Determine the apparent molar mass of the compound to the proper number of significant figures. $$\ce{Fe^3+(aq) + 3 e^- -> Fe(s)} \qquad E^\circ_\mathrm{red} = -0.04\,\mathrm{V}$$

and the standard $S^\circ$ values for these species are

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|}

iii. Calculate $\Delta H^\circ$ for the reduction of $\ce{Fe^3+}$(aq) by Al at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

b. i. Construct a Born-Haber cycle for the formation of $\ce{Al2O3}$ from its elements, showing each step in the process

$$\ce{4 Al(s) + 3 O2(g) -> 2 Al2O3(s)}$$

problems.title: Properties of the Group 14 elements
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (National Exam Part II).

Account for the following observations about the elements in Group 14 (C - Pb) and their compounds in terms of bonding principles.

a. Carbon (in the form of diamond) and silicon have the same tetrahedral structure but very pure silicon is a semiconductor while diamond is an electrical insulator.

b. Carbon and silicon both form tetrachlorides, but while $\ce{CCl4}$ does not react with $\ce{H2O}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\ce{SiCl4}$ reacts violently with $\ce{H2O}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

c. Carbon forms compounds containing chains of carbon atoms but the tendency of the elements in the family to bond to one another in this fashion decreases with increasing atomic number.

d. Germanium, tin, and lead form stable chlorides in which they exhibit oxidation states of $+2$ and $+4$ but the $+4$ state decreases in stability relative to the $+2$ state with increasing atomic number.

problems.title: Accounting for chemical kinetics observations

b. For most chemical reactions the initial reaction rate is faster than the rates at later times.

c. $1\,\mathrm{M}$ solutions of compounds A and B decompose at identical initial rates at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. At $15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ a $1\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of compound B shows a higher initial decomposition rate than a $1\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of compound A at that temperature.

problems.title: Periodic trends and bonding in elements

Account for the following observations in terms of atomic structure, intermolecular forces, or intramolecular forces.

a. The stable form of nitrogen is a diatomic molecule with a low boiling point while the most stable form of phosphorus is a network solid at room temperature.

b. The melting points of the Group I elements decrease with increasing atomic number (Li to Cs) whereas the melting points of the Group 17 elements increase with increasing atomic number (F to I).

c. The first ionization energies of the Group II elements decrease with increasing atomic number. The first three elements (Be, Mg, Ca) show a greater change ($899$ to $590\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$) than the latter three (Ca, Sr, Ba) ($590$ to $503\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$).

problems.title: Substitution reactions of bromobutane isomers

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2Br} \qquad \ce{CH3CH2CHBrCH3} \qquad \ce{(CH3)3CBr}$$

a. Which of these alkyl bromides reacts most rapidly with $\ce{OH^-}$? Outline your reasoning.

b. These substitution reactions may occur by either a uni-molecular (1) or a bi-molecular (2) mechanism.

$$\text{(1)}\quad \ce{RBr -> R+ + Br^-} \qquad \ce{R+ + OH^- -> ROH}$$

$$\text{(2)}\quad \ce{RBr + OH^- -> ROH + Br^-}$$

Predict which of the above alkyl bromides is most likely to react via a uni-molecular mechanism and outline your reasoning.

c. State the properties of a solvent that would promote the uni-molecular mechanism. Outline your reasoning.

d. Write the structure of the fourth structural isomer of $\ce{C4H9Br}$. To which of the original three compounds is its reactivity most comparable? Outline your reasoning.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2012-3-8-fig1.png

one of the mechanisms in b. forms a product with inverted configuration while the other gives a mixture of stereoisomeric products. Assign each of these results to one of the mechanisms in b. and outline your reasoning.

problems.title: Copper compound: combustion, titration, freezing point
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (National Exam Part II).

A compound contains only C, H, O and Cu. It is analyzed for its carbon and hydrogen content by combustion. The copper content is obtained by reacting it with $\ce{I^-}$ according to equation (1),

$$\ce{(1)\ 2 Cu^2+(aq) + 5 I^-(aq) -> 2 CuI(s) + I3^-(aq)}$$

and reacting the $\ce{I3^-}$ formed with standard thiosulfate, $\ce{S2O3^2-}$ according to equation (2).

$$\ce{(2)\ I3^-(aq) + 2 S2O3^2-(aq) -> 3 I^-(aq) + S4O6^2-(aq)}$$

a. The combustion of a $0.250\,\mathrm{g}$ sample of the compound produces $0.504\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{CO2}$ and $0.0743\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{H2O}$. Determine the mass percentages of carbon and hydrogen in the compound.

b. In the analysis for $\ce{Cu^2+}$, a $0.115\,\mathrm{g}$ sample of the compound is reacted with concentrated nitric acid, evaporated to dryness and the residue is dissolved in $\ce{H2O}$. The $\ce{Cu^2+}$ in the resulting solution is reacted with excess $\ce{I^-}$ and the resulting $\ce{I3^-}$ is titrated with $0.0320\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{S2O3^2-}$, requiring $11.75\,\mathrm{mL}$.

i. Name the indicator used for the titration of $\ce{I3^-}$ with $\ce{S2O3^2-}$ and describe the color change observed.

ii. Determine the moles of $\ce{Cu^2+}$ and calculate the mass percentage of Cu in the compound.

c. Find the mass percentage of oxygen and write the empirical formula for the compound.

d. A solution prepared by dissolving $0.100\,\mathrm{g}$ of this compound in $15.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of benzene, $\ce{C6H6}$, freezes at $5.436\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Find the molar mass and molecular formula of the compound. [$\ce{C6H6}$ m.p. $= 5.490\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $k_\mathrm{f} = 4.90\,^\circ\mathrm{C\cdot m^{-1}}$]

problems.title: Thermodynamics of liquid and gaseous benzene
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (National Exam Part II).

Some thermodynamic properties of liquid and gaseous benzene are given below.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & \Delta H_\mathrm{f}^\circ,\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} & S^\circ,\ \mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}} & \Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{combustion},\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} \\
\hline
\ce{C6H6}(l) & 48.7 & 173.3 & -3273 \\
\hline
\ce{C6H6}(g) & 82.9 & 269.0 & \text{NA} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Calculate the vapor pressure of benzene at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in $\mathrm{mm\,Hg}$.

b. Calculate the enthalpy change associated with the hypothetical reaction: $\ce{C6H6}(l) \rightarrow 6\,\ce{C}(s) + 3\,\ce{H2}(g)$ for $1.50\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{C6H6}$.

c. Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of one mole of benzene.

d. Use the bond energies below to calculate an estimated bond energy of the carbon-carbon bonds in benzene.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Bond} & \ce{C-H} & \ce{C-O} & \ce{C=O} & \ce{C#O} & \ce{H-O} & \ce{O-O} & \ce{O=O} \\
\hline
\text{Energy, kJ/mol} & 414 & 351 & 799 & 1070 & 464 & 142 & 498 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

e. $1.50\,\mathrm{g}$ of benzene is burned in a bomb calorimeter with a heat capacity of $5.99\,\mathrm{kJ/^\circ C}$ submerged in $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water at $22.50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Determine the final temperature of the system. [Specific heat of $\ce{H2O}(l) = 4.18\,\mathrm{J\cdot g^{-1}\cdot ^\circ C^{-1}}$]

problems.title: First-order decomposition of peroxynitric acid

The thermal decomposition of peroxynitric acid, $\ce{HO2NO2}$, has been studied and found to be first-order. The rate constant was determined to be $2.1\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $331\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1.1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $342\,\mathrm{K}$.

a. Calculate the half-life of $\ce{HO2NO2}$ at $331\,\mathrm{K}$ in seconds.

b. For a sample of $\ce{HO2NO2}$ with an initial concentration of $7.1\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$, calculate the concentration of $\ce{HO2NO2}$ after $0.40$ minutes at $331\,\mathrm{K}$.

c. Sketch a graph for the decomposition of $\ce{HO2NO2}$ at $331\,\mathrm{K}$ for three half-lives and predict the fraction remaining after five half-lives.

d. Calculate the activation energy of the reaction.

problems.title: Gas-phase equilibrium of XCl3
problems.problem:

A $0.0343\,\mathrm{mol}$ sample of $\ce{XCl3(g)}$ is added to an evacuated $1.50\,\mathrm{L}$ glass bulb. The bulb is sealed, heated to $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the following equilibrium is established: $\ce{2 XCl3(g) <=> 2 X(g) + 3 Cl2(g)}$

At equilibrium, the final pressure in the bulb is $0.800\,\mathrm{atm}$.

a. Calculate the pressure of $\ce{XCl3(g)}$ in the bulb at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ if no reaction had occurred.

b. Calculate the equilibrium partial pressures of

i. $\ce{XCl3(g)}$,

ii. $\ce{X(g)}$,

iii. $\ce{Cl2(g)}$.

c. Determine the value at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ of:

i. $K_\mathrm{p}$.

ii. $\Delta G^\circ$ in $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

d. Calculate the value of $K_\mathrm{c}$ at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

e. Write an expression that can be used to solve for the concentration of $\ce{XCl3}$ at equilibrium when $0.0500\,\mathrm{mole}$ of $\ce{XCl3}$ is placed in an evacuated $2.00\,\mathrm{L}$ glass bulb at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. You need not solve this expression.

a. Calcium sulfite is heated to a high temperature in a vacuum.

b. Solutions of sodium oxalate and acidified solution potassium permanganate are mixed.

c. Solutions of magnesium sulfate and barium hydroxide are mixed.

d. Gaseous dimethylamine and hydrogen chloride are mixed.

e. Toluene is reacted with chlorine in the presence of aluminum chloride.

problems.title: Structure and NMR of SF3Cl

Consider the highly reactive molecule $\ce{SF3Cl}$.

a. Draw all of the possible structures of $\ce{SF3Cl}$ with S as the central atom.

b. Use VSEPR theory to predict the most stable structure in a. and justify your answer.

c. Recent calculations predict that the two structures that are lowest in energy differ by about $0.2\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Identify the second lowest energy structure and justify your answer.

d. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy can be used to distinguish between atoms in different environments in a molecule. State and account for the number of unique F-19 signals if $^{19}\mathrm{F}$ NMR were carried out on $\ce{SF3Cl}$ at

i. a low temperature (e.g. $-80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)

ii. room temperature in solution.

e. While selenium and tellurium can potentially form $\ce{SeF3Cl}$ and $\ce{TeF3Cl}$, an $\ce{OF3Cl}$ species is not known even though oxygen has the same valence electron configuration. Account for this difference in the behavior of oxygen.

problems.title: Ideal and non-ideal binary solutions
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (National Exam Part II).

Consider two solutions, each of which contains two volatile components. The vapor pressure of each of these components at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is given in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Substance} & \ce{CCl4} & \ce{CHCl3} & \ce{CH3C(O)CH3} \\
\hline
\text{Vapor pressure at } 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C},\ \text{torr} & 98.8 & 172.5 & 222 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Solution 1 consists of chloroform and carbon tetrachloride, which form an ideal solution.

i. Describe an ideal solution in terms of the interactions of the component molecules and explain why $\ce{CCl4}$ and $\ce{CHCl3}$ form an ideal solution.

ii. Sketch a graph of vapor pressure vs. mole fraction $\ce{CHCl3}$ for a $\ce{CHCl3}$-$\ce{CCl4}$ solution at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and predict the vapor pressure of a solution that is $0.30$ mole fraction $\ce{CHCl3}$.

iii. Describe how the composition of the vapor over this solution compares with the composition of the solution. Justify your answer.

b. Propanone, $\ce{CH3C(O)CH3}$, and chloroform mix with the release of heat.

i. Describe or sketch clearly the interaction between the propanone and chloroform molecules that is responsible for the heat release.

ii. Use the axes from a. to sketch a graph of vapor pressure vs. mole fraction $\ce{CHCl3}$ and account for its appearance.

problems.title: Nitrogen oxides and photochemical smog
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (National Exam Part II).

Nitrogen forms many oxides, some of which are significant in the formation of photochemical smog. The $\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $\Delta G^\circ_{\mathrm{f}}$ values for several of these nitrogen oxides are given in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & \Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{f}},\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} & \Delta G^\circ_{\mathrm{f}},\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} \\
\hline
\ce{NO2(g)} & 33.85 & 51.84 \\
\hline
\ce{N2O4(g)} & 9.66 & 98.29 \\
\hline
\ce{NO(g)} & 90.37 & 86.71 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Calculate the enthalpy and free energy changes at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for the

i. formation of $\ce{NO2(g)}$ from $\ce{NO(g)}$ and $\ce{O2(g)}$.

ii. dimerization of $\ce{NO2(g)}$ to form $\ce{N2O4(g)}$.

b. Calculate the equilibrium constant for the dimerization of $\ce{NO2(g)}$ at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

c. For an atmospheric concentration of $\ce{NO2}$ equal to $30.\ \mathrm{ppb}$ ($1.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{M}$) at $298\,\mathrm{K}$, calculate the equilibrium concentration of $\ce{N2O4}$.

d. If the atmospheric temperature increases to $43.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and equilibrium is established, does the new concentration of nitrogen dioxide formed from conversion of $\ce{N2O4}$ exceed the EPA limit of $53\,\mathrm{ppb}$ ($2.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{M}$)? Explain.

e. The positive $\Delta G^\circ_{\mathrm{f}}$ for $\ce{NO2}$ indicates that its decomposition to form the elements $\ce{N2}$ and $\ce{O2}$ is spontaneous. Suggest a reason that this process does not occur to a significant extent in the atmosphere once $\ce{NO2}$ has been formed.

problems.title: Solubility equilibria of barium and lead fluorides

a. Calculate the molar solubility of barium fluoride at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

b. Explain how adding each of the following substances affects the solubility of $\ce{BaF2}$ in water.

c. In an experiment to determine the $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ of $\ce{PbF2}$ a student starts with $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{Pb(NO3)2}$ and $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KF}$ and uses the method of serial dilutions to find the lowest $[\ce{Pb^2+}]$ and $[\ce{F-}]$ that form a precipitate when mixed. If the student uses the concentration of the ions in the combined solution to determine $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$, will the value of $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ calculated be too large, too small or just right? Explain.

$K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ for $\ce{PbF2} = 4.0 \times 10^{-8}$

d. i. In a solution of $0.010\,\mathrm{M}$ barium nitrate and $0.010\,\mathrm{M}$ lead(II) nitrate, which will precipitate first, $\ce{BaF2}$ or $\ce{PbF2}$, as $\ce{NaF(s)}$ is added? Assume volume changes are negligible. Explain (support your answer with calculations).

\text{Experiment} & [\ce{NO}],\ \mathrm{M} & [\ce{O2}],\ \mathrm{M} & \text{Initial Rate of } \ce{NO2} \text{ formation},\ \mathrm{M\cdot s^{-1}} \\

problems.title: Chemistry of the Group 13 elements

This question concerns the chemistry of the Group 13 elements (B - Tl). Base your answers on principles of atomic structure and bonding.

problems.title: Acetate buffer and chloroacetate comparison

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2016-3-4-fig1.png

The reaction was studied at $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and was found to be first-order in $\mathbf{X}$ under all conditions. The amount of $\mathbf{X}$ was monitored over time in two different buffer solutions and the following data were obtained:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Time, s} & [\mathbf{X}],\ \mathrm{M}\ (\mathrm{pH} = 10.10\ \text{buffer}) & [\mathbf{X}],\ \mathrm{M}\ (\mathrm{pH} = 10.60\ \text{buffer}) \\

0 & 3.61 \times 10^{-4} & 3.59 \times 10^{-4} \\

600 & & 1.78 \times 10^{-4} \\

740 & 2.75 \times 10^{-4} & \\

$$\mathrm{rate} = k'[\mathbf{X}]$$

\ce{I2(s) + 2 e^- -> 2 I^-(aq)} & & E^\circ = +0.540\,\mathrm{V}
\end{array}$$

a. Calculate the number of moles of copper that dissolve if $1.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{CuI(s)}$ is suspended in $1.00\,\mathrm{L}$ of solution.

b. Calculate the minimum number of moles of $\ce{NaI}$ that would need to be added to the mixture in (a) to fully dissolve the $\ce{CuI}$. You may assume that the volume remains $1.00\,\mathrm{L}$.

c. Calculate $K_\mathrm{eq}$ for the (favorable) disproportionation of aqueous $\ce{Cu+}$ ion in neutral solution:

$$\ce{2 Cu+(aq) <=> Cu^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)}$$

d. Copper(II) iodide, $\ce{CuI2}$, is not stable. Write a reasonable chemical reaction that describes the decomposition of $\ce{CuI2}$ in aqueous solution, and show that this is a spontaneous reaction under standard conditions.

problems.title: Kinetics of ozone decomposition
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (National Exam Part II).

The initial rate of decomposition of ozone to molecular oxygen has been examined under a variety of conditions by measuring the change in pressure as the reaction takes place.

$$\ce{2 O3(g) -> 3 O2(g)}$$

At $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in the presence of relatively small amounts of $\ce{O3}$ compared to $\ce{O2}$ (present in constant amount), the following data were obtained:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
p(\ce{O3}),\ \mathrm{mm\,Hg} & \Delta P/\Delta t,\ (\mathrm{mm\,Hg})\,\mathrm{s^{-1}} \\
\hline
7.9 & 1.21 \times 10^{-3} \\
\hline
17.7 & 5.8 \times 10^{-3} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. If the pressure changes at a rate of $1.21 \times 10^{-3}\,(\mathrm{mm\,Hg})\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, what is the rate of disappearance of $\ce{O3}$ in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$?

b. What is the order in $\ce{O3}$ under these conditions?

Under slightly different conditions, with the initial pressures of $\ce{O3}$ held constant, the initial rates were measured as a function of $\ce{O2}$ pressure at $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
p(\ce{O2}),\ \mathrm{mm\,Hg} & \Delta P/\Delta t,\ (\mathrm{mm\,Hg})\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\ \text{at } 90\,^\circ\mathrm{C} & \Delta P/\Delta t,\ (\mathrm{mm\,Hg})\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\ \text{at } 100\,^\circ\mathrm{C} \\
\hline
200 & 3.30 \times 10^{-3} & 7.4 \times 10^{-3} \\
\hline
400 & 1.45 \times 10^{-3} & 3.64 \times 10^{-3} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

c. What is the order in $\ce{O2}$?

d. What is the activation energy for the reaction?

e. The following mechanism has been proposed for the reaction:

$$\ce{O3(g) <=>[k_1][k_{-1}] O2(g) + O(g)}$$

$$\ce{O(g) + O3(g) ->[k_2] 2 O2(g)}$$

Using the steady-state approximation, derive the rate law predicted by this mechanism. Under what circumstances, if any, is this consistent with the experimental data?

problems.title: Thermodynamics of NO2 dimerization
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (National Exam Part II).

Consider the dimerization of nitrogen dioxide:

$$\ce{2 NO2(g) <=> N2O4(g)}$$

Thermodynamic data are given below for the gaseous species at $298\,\mathrm{K}$, except for the heats of vaporization, which are for the liquids:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & \ce{NO2} & \ce{N2O4} \\
\hline
\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{f},\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 33.2 & 11.1 \\
\hline
S^\circ,\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & 240.1 & 304.4 \\
\hline
C_\mathrm{p},\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & 37.2 & 79.2 \\
\hline
\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{vap},\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 27.7 & 38.1 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$, $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$, and $\Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$ for the dimerization of $\ce{NO2(g)}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

b. Calculate $K_\mathrm{eq}$ for the dimerization of $\ce{NO2(g)}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

c. Would $K_\mathrm{eq}$ for the dimerization at $308\,\mathrm{K}$ be greater than, less than, or equal to $K_\mathrm{eq}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$? Justify your answer based on the above data.

d. Would $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$ at $308\,\mathrm{K}$ be greater than, less than, or equal to $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$? Justify your answer based on the above data.

problems.title: Silicon unit cell and semiconductors
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (National Exam Part II).

Silicon is an industrially important semiconductor with the cubic unit cell shown below (Si atoms represented as black spheres):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2017-3-6-fig1.png

a. How many Si atoms are contained in this unit cell?

b. The length of the edge of the unit cell is $0.543\,\mathrm{nm}$. Calculate the density of silicon in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

Semiconductors like Si have an electronic structure characterized by a band of nominally filled orbitals (the “valence band”) separated from a band of nominally empty orbitals (the “conduction band”) by an energy gap called the “band gap” of the semiconductor. Conduction arises in a pure semiconductor when there is thermal promotion of an electron from the valence to the conduction band; both the electron in the conduction band and the vacancy (“hole”) in the valence band are efficient carriers for electrical conduction.

c. Diamond, silicon, and germanium all have the same structure, but the band gap decreases in the order C (diamond) $\gg$ Si $>$ Ge. Explain the trend in the size of the band gap.

d. Substituting just a few parts per million of B into Si results in a dramatic increase of electrical conductivity compared to ultrapure Si. Explain why.

problems.title: Binary fluorides of oxygen and sulfur
problems.problem:

a. Draw the Lewis structure of dioxygen difluoride, $\ce{O2F2}$, and sketch or describe the three-dimensional shape of this polar molecule.

b. Explain why the O$-$F bonds in dioxygen difluoride, $\ce{O2F2}$ ($157.5\,\mathrm{pm}$) are much longer than those in oxygen difluoride, $\ce{OF2}$ ($140.5\,\mathrm{pm}$).

c. Disulfur difluoride, $\ce{S2F2}$, exists as two structural isomers. One isomer is analogous in structure to dioxygen difluoride, $\ce{O2F2}$, but the second, more thermodynamically stable isomer, has a structure in which the two sulfur atoms are in different chemical environments. Draw a Lewis structure of the more stable isomer of disulfur difluoride, $\ce{S2F2}$, and sketch or describe its three-dimensional shape.

d. Sulfur difluoride, $\ce{SF2}$, is very unstable, converting to disulfur tetrafluoride, $\ce{S2F4}$, in which all four fluorines are in different environments. Clearly show a chemically reasonable three-dimensional structure of disulfur tetrafluoride, $\ce{S2F4}$, and explain how the structure accounts for the inequivalence of all four fluorine atoms.

e. Sulfur tetrafluoride, $\ce{SF4}$ (bp $-38\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), has a higher boiling point than sulfur hexafluoride, $\ce{SF6}$ (bp $-64\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Explain why sulfur tetrafluoride, $\ce{SF4}$, is less volatile than sulfur hexafluoride, $\ce{SF6}$.

ii. the reaction of the yellow solution with the sodium thiosulfate solution.

ii. Adding an electron to a gas-phase Be atom requires energy, while adding an electron to a gas-phase Ba atom releases a small amount of energy ($14\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).

iii. $\ce{BeCl2(s)}$ has a more positive $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{f}$ ($-496.2\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) than $\ce{BaCl2(s)}$ ($-858.6\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$)

iv. Solid $\ce{BeCl2}$ adopts the structure shown on the left, while solid $\ce{BaCl2}$ adopts the structure shown on the right (metal = black spheres, chlorine = gray spheres).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2019-3-6-fig1.png

b. In the vapor phase, $\ce{BeCl2}$ exists as a mixture of $\ce{BeCl2}$ monomers and $\ce{Be2Cl4}$ dimers. Draw or clearly describe the geometries of these two gas-phase species.

c. At $800\,\mathrm{K}$, $K_\mathrm{p}$ for dimerization of $\ce{BeCl2(g)}$ is $2.9$.

Problem 7 (National Exam Part II).

Borazine, $\ce{B3N3H6}$, has a structure consisting of a six-membered ring with alternating $\ce{BH}$ and $\ce{NH}$ groups.

a. Draw a Lewis structure for borazine, including nonzero formal charges if needed. Show all major resonance structures of borazine.

b. Two other compounds containing boron, nitrogen, and hydrogen are $\ce{BH3NH3}$ and $\ce{BH2NH2}$. Draw Lewis structures for these two compounds, again including any formal charges and major resonance structures.

c. The $\ce{B-N}$ distances in $\ce{B3N3H6}$, $\ce{BH3NH3}$, and $\ce{BH2NH2}$ are $139.1$, $142.9$, and $156.4\,\mathrm{pm}$ (not necessarily in that order). Assign each $\ce{B-N}$ distances to the proper compound and explain your reasoning.

d. Typically, when one replaces a hydrogen attached to $\ce{N}$ with a $\ce{CH3}$ group, the boiling point of the compound decreases. For example, piperazine has a normal boiling point of $146\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ while $N$-methylpiperazine has a normal boiling point of $138\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Explain this observation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2019-3-7-fig1.png

e. In contrast to the situation in (d), when one $\ce{N-H}$ group in borazine (bp $= 55\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) is changed to an $\ce{N-CH3}$ group, the normal boiling point of $N$-methylborazine increases significantly, to $84\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. problems.title: Mond process for nickel tetracarbonyl
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (National Exam Part II).

The Mond process was used in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to purify nickel metal away from impurities such as iron and cobalt. The process relies on the facile reaction of nickel with carbon monoxide to form volatile nickel tetracarbonyl, which can be separated from the solid impurities:

$$\ce{Ni(s) + 4 CO(g) -> Ni(CO)4(g)}$$

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & \ce{Ni(s)} & \ce{Ni(g)} & \ce{CO(g)} & \ce{Ni(CO)4(g)} \\
\hline
\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{f}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 0 & 430.1 & -110.5 & -607 \\
\hline
S^\circ\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & 30 & 182.2 & 198 & 417 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Draw or clearly describe the three-dimensional arrangement of the atoms in $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$.

b. Calculate the average bond dissociation enthalpy for the nickel-carbon bonds in $\ce{Ni(CO)4(g)}$.

c. Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$ for the production of $\ce{Ni(CO)4(g)}$ by the Mond process.

d. The boiling point of $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$ at $1\,\mathrm{bar}$ pressure is $42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and its heat of vaporization is $29.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{f}$ and $S^\circ$ for $\ce{Ni(CO)4(l)}$.

e. After the $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$ vapor has been separated from the solid impurities, $\ce{Ni}$ metal is recovered by heating the $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$ to high temperature, causing it to re-form nickel metal and carbon monoxide. At $230\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, what is the equilibrium pressure of $\ce{Ni(CO)4(g)}$ in the presence of nickel metal, assuming that the carbon monoxide pressure is maintained at $0.10\,\mathrm{bar}$?

problems.title: Kinetics of bromine monoxide decomposition
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (National Exam Part II).

Gas-phase bromine monoxide, $\ce{BrO}$, decomposes according to two possible pathways:

$$\ce{2 BrO(g) -> O2(g) + 2 Br(g)} \qquad (4a)$$

$$\ce{2 BrO(g) -> O2(g) + Br2(g)} \qquad (4b)$$

The reaction can be studied by generating $\ce{BrO(g)}$ by using a laser. If this is carried out in the presence of excess ozone, then any $\ce{Br(g)}$ that is present reacts with ozone to produce bromine monoxide much more rapidly than either reaction 4a or 4b.

$$\ce{Br(g) + O3(g) -> BrO(g) + O2(g)} \qquad \textit{fast}$$

The disappearance of $\ce{BrO(g)}$ was studied spectrophotometrically at both $267\,\mathrm{K}$ and $298\,\mathrm{K}$, either in the absence of excess ozone (open squares) or in the presence of excess ozone (open circles). The reciprocal of the concentration of $\ce{BrO}$ as a function of time is graphed below for the four experiments.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2020-3-4-fig1.png

a. What is the reaction order in $\ce{BrO}$ for its decomposition in the absence of $\ce{O3}$? Justify your answer based on the experimental data.

b. A sample of $\ce{BrO}$ in $\ce{N2}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ with an initial concentration of $4.0 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{molecules\,cm^{-3}}$ is prepared. How much time will it take for the $\ce{BrO}$ concentration to decay to half its original value?

c. Is the observed decomposition of $\ce{BrO}$ faster or slower in the presence of ozone? Justify your answer based on the experimental data and provide a chemical explanation for the observed difference.

d. Calculate the values of $k_\mathrm{4a}$ and $k_\mathrm{4b}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

e. Calculate the activation energy for the decomposition of $\ce{BrO}$ in the presence of ozone.

A solution is made by adding some $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ to water, followed by enough sulfuric acid to make the $\mathrm{pH} = 1.00$. Two platinum electrodes are then placed in the solution (which has a total volume of $0.500\,\mathrm{L}$) and the solution is electrolyzed at a constant current of $0.120\,\mathrm{A}$, separately capturing any gases that are evolved at the two electrodes.

Initially, gas is evolved at the anode, but no gas is evolved at the cathode. However, after $10.0\,\mathrm{min}$ of electrolysis, gas evolution begins at the cathode as well, and eventually the total volume of gas evolved at the cathode is equal to the total volume of gas evolved at the anode.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c||c|c|}
\hline
\text{Half-Reaction} & E^\circ,\ \mathrm{V} & \text{Half-Reaction} & E^\circ,\ \mathrm{V} \\
\hline
\ce{Cu+(aq) + e- -> Cu(s)} & 0.518 & \ce{Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2 e- -> Cu(s)} & 0.337 \\
\hline
\ce{O2(g) + 2 H+(aq) + 2 e- -> H2O2(aq)} & 1.780 & \ce{O2(g) + 4 H+(aq) + 4 e- -> 2 H2O(l)} & 1.229 \\
\hline
\ce{2 H+(aq) + e- -> H2(g)} & 0.000 & & \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Write the balanced reaction that takes place initially in this electrolytic cell.

b. How many moles of copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate were initially added to the solution?

c. What is the initial cell potential for this reaction at $298\,\mathrm{K}$? (In air, the partial pressure of $\ce{O2(g)}$ is $0.20\,\mathrm{bar}$ and the partial pressure of $\ce{H2(g)}$ may be taken to be $10^{-4}\,\mathrm{bar}$.)

d. As the electrolysis proceeds (before $t = 10.0\,\mathrm{min}$), will this cell potential become more positive, more negative, or remain unchanged? Explain your answer.

e. What gas is evolved at the anode? What gas is evolved at the cathode (after $t = 10.0\,\mathrm{min}$)?

f. At what time will the total volumes of evolved gases at the two electrodes be equal?

b. Explain why elemental silicon is a much better conductor of electricity than diamond.

d. Explain why the ionization energy of a ground-state gas-phase silicon atom ($787\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) is smaller than that of a phosphorus atom ($1012\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$), but the amount of energy released on adding an electron to a gas-phase $\ce{Si}$ atom ($144\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) is greater than that of a $\ce{P}$ atom ($71\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).

e. Explain why $\ce{SiH2(g)}$ in its ground state has no unpaired electrons, while $\ce{CH2(g)}$ in its ground state has two unpaired electrons.

problems.title: Isomers and reactions of C5H10 hydrocarbons
problems.problem:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2020-3-8-fig1.png

problems.title: NO2Cl and NO equilibrium thermodynamics
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (National Exam Part II).

The gas-phase equilibrium between nitryl chloride ($\ce{NO2Cl}$) and nitrosyl chloride ($\ce{NOCl}$) was studied:

$$\ce{NO2Cl(g) + NO(g) <=> NOCl(g) + NO2(g)} \qquad (4a)$$

The equilibrium constant for reaction 4a was measured as $K_\mathrm{4a} = 1.12 \times 10^{4}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ and $K_\mathrm{4a} = 4.68 \times 10^{3}$ at $340\,\mathrm{K}$.

a. Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{4a}$ at both $298\,\mathrm{K}$ and $340\,\mathrm{K}$.

b. Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{4a}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{4a}$ (assuming that they are essentially independent of temperature).

c. Which of the four gaseous compounds involved in this equilibrium has the lowest standard molar entropy $S^\circ$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$? Justify your choice.

d. The normal boiling point of $\ce{NOCl}$ is $-6\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Consider reaction 4b that produces liquid $\ce{NOCl}$ rather than gaseous $\ce{NOCl}$:

$$\ce{NO2Cl(g) + NO(g) <=> NOCl(l) + NO2(g)} \qquad (4b)$$

At $298\,\mathrm{K}$, how will each of the thermodynamic quantities $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{4b}$, $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{4b}$, and $\Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{4b}$ compare to the corresponding thermodynamic quantity for reaction 4a (i.e., will the quantity for 4b be greater than, less than, or equal to the quantity for 4a)? Justify your answers.

e. In experimental practice, the study of equilibrium 4a is complicated by the fact that $\ce{NO2(g)}$ is also in equilibrium with $\ce{N2O4(g)}$ according to reaction 4c under conditions where reaction 4a attains equilibrium.

$$\ce{2 NO2(g) <=> N2O4(g)} \qquad (4c)$$

Suppose that samples of $\ce{NO2Cl}$ and $\ce{NO}$ are introduced into a reaction vessel and the mixture is allowed to attain equilibrium according to reactions 4a and 4c at $320\,\mathrm{K}$. If the volume of the reaction vessel is doubled, will the number of moles of $\ce{NOCl(g)}$ increase, decrease, or stay the same after the system reattains equilibrium? Justify your answer.

\ce{N2O2(g) + H2(g) -> N2O(g) + H2O(g)} & \textit{slow, irreversible} \\

problems.title: Chlorofluorocarbon of unknown formula
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (National Exam Part II).

Compound $\mathbf{A}$ contains only carbon, fluorine, and chlorine.

a. The vapor density of $\mathbf{A}$ at $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $6.895\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$. What is the molar mass of $\mathbf{A}$?

b. Chlorofluorocarbons such as $\mathbf{A}$ react with sodium metal to convert all the chlorine present into sodium chloride. The products from the reaction of sodium with $100.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of gaseous $\mathbf{A}$ (at $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) are dissolved in water and a few drops of sodium chromate solution are added. This solution is then titrated with $0.3540\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{AgNO3}$ solution until a bright red precipitate appears, which requires $22.79\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the titrant. How many chlorine atoms are there in a molecule of $\mathbf{A}$?

c. What is the molecular formula of $\mathbf{A}$? Justify your answer.

d. There is only one known isomer of $\mathbf{A}$, compound $\mathbf{B}$. The two compounds have nearly identical boiling points, but can be distinguished by $^{19}\mathrm{F}$ NMR spectroscopy, a technique that is sensitive to small differences in the chemical environments of fluorine atoms in compounds. When analyzed by this method, compound $\mathbf{A}$ exhibits only a single type of chemical environment for fluorine, while compound $\mathbf{B}$ shows two distinct environments for its fluorine atoms. Draw structural formulas for compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ that are consistent with these observations.

b. What mole ratio of ammonia to ammonium chloride is required for the buffer to have $\mathrm{pH} = 9.20$?

c. Calculate the volume of ammonia solution and mass of ammonium chloride needed to make up $500\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the $\mathrm{pH} = 9.20$ buffer with a total concentration of nitrogen-containing species ($\ce{NH3}$ or $\ce{NH4+}$) of $0.50\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

d. To the solution described in (c) is added $10.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{AgNO3}$.

i. Some $\ce{AgCl}$ precipitates from this mixture. Justify that this is the case. The $K_\mathrm{sp}$ of $\ce{AgCl}$ is $1.8 \times 10^{-10}$ and the $K_\mathrm{f}$ of $\ce{Ag(NH3)2+}$ is $1.6 \times 10^{7}$.

ii. What is the final concentration of free $\ce{Ag+}$ in solution after this mixture achieves equilibrium?

iii. What is the mass of $\ce{AgCl}$ that precipitates from solution?

Problem 3 (National Exam Part II).

Gaseous molecular and atomic bromine have the following thermodynamic properties:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Species} & \boldsymbol{\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{f}}\ \textbf{(kJ mol}^{-1}\textbf{)} & \boldsymbol{S^\circ}\ \textbf{(J mol}^{-1}\ \textbf{K}^{-1}\textbf{)} \\
\hline
\ce{Br2}(g) & 30.9 & 245.4 \\
\hline
\ce{Br}(g) & 111.9 & 175.0 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. What is the bond dissociation enthalpy (BDE) of the bromine-bromine bond in $\ce{Br2}(g)$?

b. How many atoms of $\ce{Br}(g)$ will be present at equilibrium in a $1.00\text{-L}$ container with $0.100\,\mathrm{bar}$ of $\ce{Br2}(g)$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$?

c. The ionization energy of $\ce{Br}(g)$ is $1145.9\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, while the ionization energy of $\ce{Br2}(g)$ is $1025.1\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. What is the bond dissociation enthalpy of $\ce{Br2+}(g)$ (defined as the enthalpy of reaction of $\ce{Br2+}(g)$ to form $\ce{Br+}(g)$ and $\ce{Br}(g)$)?

d. Propose an explanation for the difference in BDE between $\ce{Br2}(g)$ and $\ce{Br2+}(g)$ in terms of the bonding in these two species.

e. The vapor pressure of liquid bromine at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ is $0.283\,\mathrm{bar}$. What is the absolute entropy $S^\circ$ of $\ce{Br2}(l)$?

f. The absolute entropies of the gas-phase atoms of the fourth period given in the table exhibit a non-monotonic pattern. Explain why the absolute entropies of $\ce{Se}(g)$ and $\ce{Br}(g)$ are larger than the absolute entropies of either $\ce{As}(g)$ or $\ce{Kr}(g)$.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & \ce{As}(g) & \ce{Se}(g) & \ce{Br}(g) & \ce{Kr}(g) \\
\hline
S^\circ,\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & 163.2 & 176.7 & 175.0 & 164.1 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

problems.title: Iodide and hydrogen peroxide clock reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (National Exam Part II).

Iodide ion reacts with hydrogen peroxide in acidic solution according to the following equation:

$$\ce{2 I-(aq) + H2O2(aq) + 2 H+(aq) -> I2(aq) + 2 H2O(l)} \qquad (4)$$

The reaction is carried out at $18.8\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in the presence of a mixture of $\ce{CH3COOH}$ and $\ce{NaOH}$ to regulate the pH, sodium thiosulfate (which reacts very rapidly with $\ce{I2}$ to form tetrathionate ions), and starch. All the components except the hydrogen peroxide are premixed, and then the hydrogen peroxide solution is added and a stopwatch is started. The solution remains colorless until it suddenly turns blue, at which point the time $t$ is recorded. The following data are obtained:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Run} & \begin{array}{c}1.0\,\mathrm{M}\\ \ce{CH3COOH},\\ \mathrm{mL}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}1.0\,\mathrm{M}\ \ce{NaOH},\\ \mathrm{mL}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}0.20\,\mathrm{M}\\ \ce{KI},\ \mathrm{mL}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}0.20\,\mathrm{M}\\ \ce{H2O2},\ \mathrm{mL}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}0.020\,\mathrm{M}\\ \ce{Na2S2O3},\\ \mathrm{mL}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Distilled}\\ \ce{H2O},\ \mathrm{mL}\end{array} & t,\ \mathrm{s} \\
\hline
\text{A} & 2.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 2.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 68.2 \\
\hline
\text{B} & 4.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 2.0 & 1.0 & 0.0 & 68.9 \\
\hline
\text{C} & 2.0 & 1.0 & 4.0 & 2.0 & 1.0 & 0.0 & 33.2 \\
\hline
\text{D} & 2.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 4.0 & 1.0 & 0.0 & 32.9 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Give a qualitative explanation for why the solution suddenly turns blue after a certain amount of time has elapsed.

b. Calculate the initial $[\ce{H+}]$ in runs A and B and explain why $[\ce{H+}]$ will not change significantly over the course of the respective reactions. (The $K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{CH3COOH}$ is $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$.)

c. The rate law for reaction (4) has the form $\mathrm{Rate} = k_4[\ce{I-}]^m[\ce{H2O2}]^n[\ce{H+}]^p$, where $m$, $n$, and $p$ are integers. What are the values of $m$, $n$, and $p$ under these experimental conditions? Briefly explain your reasoning.

d. What is the value of the rate constant $k_4$ for this reaction?

e. The following mechanism for reaction (4) has been proposed:

$$\begin{array}{lr}
\ce{H2O2(aq) + H+(aq) <=> H3O2+(aq)} & (\textit{fast, unfavorable}) \\
\ce{H3O2+(aq) + I-(aq) -> HOI(aq) + H2O(l)} & (\textit{slow}) \\
\ce{HOI(aq) + H+(aq) <=> H2OI+(aq)} & (\textit{fast, unfavorable}) \\
\ce{H2OI+(aq) + I-(aq) -> I2(aq) + H2O(l)} & (\textit{fast})
\end{array}$$

Is this mechanism consistent with the given data? Justify your answer.

f. The experiments are repeated under the same conditions as Runs A and B above, except that phosphoric acid ($\ce{H3PO4}$, $K_\mathrm{a} = 7.6 \times 10^{-3}$) is substituted for acetic acid. The observed times for the solutions to turn blue with this substitution are $46.7\,\mathrm{s}$ and $31.5\,\mathrm{s}$, respectively. Propose an interpretation for these observations.

A galvanic cell is constructed at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ with one half-cell consisting of a $10.00\,\mathrm{g}$ silver wire immersed in $1.00\,\mathrm{L}$ of a $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of silver nitrate and the second half-cell consisting of a $20.00\,\mathrm{g}$ copper plate immersed in $1.00\,\mathrm{L}$ of a $0.200\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of copper(II) sulfate.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Half-reaction} & E^\circ,\ \mathrm{V} \\

\ce{Ag+(aq) + e- -> Ag(s)} & 0.800 \\
\hline
\ce{Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2 e- -> Cu(s)} & 0.337 \\

a. What voltage is measured for this galvanic cell?

b. The cell is discharged at a constant current of $0.150\,\mathrm{A}$ until the mass of the silver electrode is equal to the mass of the copper electrode. How much time does this take?

Problem 1 (National Exam Part II).

$\mathbf{A}$ is an ionic compound that contains only the elements hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2023-3-1-fig1.png

b. When a $1.000\text{-g}$ sample of $\mathbf{A}$ is heated at $230\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in an evacuated $1.50\,\mathrm{L}$ vessel, it decomposes into gaseous products, giving a final pressure of $784\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}$. How many moles of gas are formed in this reaction?

c. If the gases produced from the decomposition of $1.000\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ are instead first passed through a column packed with magnesium perchlorate (which strongly absorbs water vapor) and then collected at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a pressure of $755\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}$, the total volume of gas is $308\,\mathrm{mL}$. How many moles of gas are collected in this experiment?

d. What is the formula of $\mathbf{A}$? Explain your reasoning.

e. Write Lewis structures for the cation and the anion present in $\mathbf{A}$ and for the product(s) of its decomposition at $230\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Your Lewis structures should include all bonds, lone pairs, and nonzero formal charges. You should show all significant resonance structures for each species.

problems.title: Acidity of aqua zinc ions and zinc hydroxide solubility

Problem 2 (National Exam Part II).

When water is bound to a metal ion, its acidity increases. For example, the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{Zn^{2+}}(aq)$ is $8.96$.

a. Calculate the pH of a $0.010\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of zinc nitrate, $\ce{Zn(NO3)2}$.

b. Calculate the pH of a $0.010\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of zinc acetate, $\ce{Zn(CH3COO)2}$. The $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of $\ce{CH3COOH}$ is $4.75$.

c. Zinc hydroxide is sparingly soluble, with $K_\mathrm{sp} = 4.5 \times 10^{-17}$. Calculate the pH of a solution of water saturated with solid $\ce{Zn(OH)2}$.

d. Under what circumstances, if any, will a solution of zinc acetate spontaneously form a precipitate of $\ce{Zn(OH)2}$? If precipitation is possible, specify the circumstances under which it is spontaneous. If it is not possible, justify why not.

e. Zinc also forms a complex ion, $\ce{Zn(OH)4^{2-}}$, with $K_\mathrm{f} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}$. Calculate the solubility of $\ce{Zn(OH)2}$ in a solution with $\mathrm{pH} = 12.00$.

problems.title: Thermochemistry of hydrogen combustion
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (National Exam Part II).

Hydrogen gas reacts with oxygen gas to give water vapor with $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{rxn} = -241.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{rxn} = -44.5\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

$$\ce{H2}(g) + 0.5\,\ce{O2}(g) \rightarrow \ce{H2O}(g)$$

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Species} & S^\circ,\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & C_\mathrm{p},\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\
\hline
\ce{H2O}(g) & ??? & 4.18 \\
\hline
\ce{H2}(g) & 130.7 & 14.4 \\
\hline
\ce{O2}(g) & 205.2 & 0.92 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Calculate $S^\circ$ of $\ce{H2O}(g)$.

b. The bond dissociation enthalpy (BDE) of an average $\ce{O-H}$ bond in water is $463\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and the BDE of the $\ce{H-H}$ bond in $\ce{H2}$ is $436\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. What is the BDE of the $\ce{O=O}$ bond in $\ce{O2}$?

c. $0.100\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{H2}(g)$ and $0.100\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{O2}(g)$, both initially at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, react completely in a sealed vessel that is maintained at $1\,\mathrm{bar}$ pressure. The vessel is machined as part of a $1.00\text{-kg}$ block of aluminum ($C_\mathrm{p} = 0.89\,\mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$), which efficiently absorbs the heat generated in the reaction but which is well insulated from its surroundings. What is the final temperature of the aluminum block and the contents of the reaction vessel? Assume that $C_\mathrm{p}$ and $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{rxn}$ are independent of temperature.

d. Humid air at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ has an overall pressure of $1.0\,\mathrm{bar}$ and is $20.\,\mathrm{vol\%}$ $\ce{O2}$ and $3.1\,\mathrm{vol\%}$ $\ce{H2O}$. What is the minimum volume percentage of $\ce{H2}(g)$ in humid air necessary for its combustion to be spontaneous?

e. The lower flammability limit (LFL) of a substance is its minimum volumetric concentration needed to propagate a flame under a given set of conditions. The LFL of hydrogen gas in humid air is approximately $4\%$. Account for the difference between your answer in part d and the experimental value for the LFL.

problems.title: Vapor pressure and freezing of aqueous magnesium chloride

a. $0.880\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{MgCl2}$ is added to $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ liquid water at $0.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the vapor pressure of this solution.

b. The enthalpy of sublimation of ice is $51.1\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $0.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the enthalpy of vaporization of liquid water is $45.1\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $0.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming these enthalpies are independent of temperature, calculate the temperature at which pure ice has the same vapor pressure as the magnesium chloride solution at $0.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ calculated in part a.

c. At the freezing point temperature of the aqueous magnesium chloride solution, the vapor pressure of the solution is equal to the vapor pressure of pure ice. Explain why this statement is true.

d. Using the principle enunciated in part c, calculate the freezing point temperature of the solution of $0.880\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{MgCl2}$ dissolved in $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ water.

e. The temperature calculated in part d is the temperature of the system when the first solid appears at equilibrium as the system is cooled. As more solid is formed, do you expect the temperature to increase, decrease, or remain constant? Briefly justify your choice.

Problem 6 (National Exam Part II).

Consider the properties of the group 1 elements, whose valence shell electron configuration is $ns^1$, in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Element } M & n & \begin{array}{c}\text{First ionization}\\ \text{energy, kJ mol}^{-1}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Energy required to excite the valence}\\ \text{electron to the } (n+1)s \text{ orbital, kJ mol}^{-1}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Molar density of}\\ \text{solid } M\text{Cl, mol cm}^{-3}\end{array} \\
\hline
\text{H} & 1 & 1312 & 984 & 0.0403 \\
\hline
\text{Li} & 2 & 520 & 325 & 0.0507 \\
\hline
\text{Na} & 3 & 496 & 308 & 0.0371 \\
\hline
\text{K} & 4 & 420 & 252 & 0.0266 \\
\hline
\text{Rb} & 5 & 403 & 241 & 0.0232 \\
\hline
\text{Cs} & 6 & 376 & 222 & 0.0237 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Rationalize the observed trend in first ionization energies with increasing $n$.

b. Suppose a hydrogen atom were excited to its $2s^1$ state. If that excited state atom were to transfer its electron to $\ce{Cs+}$ to form a ground-state Cs atom, how much energy would that reaction absorb or release?

c. All but one of the atoms listed in the table have an excited state that is significantly lower in energy than the $(n+1)s^1$ state described in the table. Explain this observation, noting which atom is the exception and why.

d. All but one of the atoms listed in the table have an excited state that is modestly higher in energy ($38 - 55\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) than the $(n+1)s^1$ state described in the table. Explain this observation, noting which atom is the exception and why.

problems.title: Carbonyl azide, diazirinone and bond enthalpies
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (National Exam Part II).

Flash vacuum pyrolysis of carbonyl azide ($\ce{CON6}$) at $420\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gives low yields of a cyclic compound, diazirinone, as shown in the equation below. Note that the illustrations of carbonyl azide and diazirinone correctly show the connectivity of the atoms but are NOT correct Lewis structures. The bond dissociation enthalpies (BDE, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) of various bonds among carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen are given in the table.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2024-3-7-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Bond} & \text{BDE, kJ mol}^{-1} & \text{Bond} & \text{BDE, kJ mol}^{-1} & \text{Bond} & \text{BDE, kJ mol}^{-1} & \text{Bond} & \text{BDE, kJ mol}^{-1} \\
\hline
\mathrm{C{-}O} & 350 & \mathrm{C{-}N} & 290 & \mathrm{N{-}N} & 160 & \mathrm{N{-}O} & 200 \\
\hline
\mathrm{C{=}O} & 741 & \mathrm{C{=}N} & 615 & \mathrm{N{=}N} & 418 & \mathrm{N{=}O} & 480 \\
\hline
\mathrm{C{\equiv}O} & 1080 & \mathrm{C{\equiv}N} & 891 & \mathrm{N{\equiv}N} & 949 & & \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

a. Draw complete Lewis structures for carbonyl azide and for diazirinone, including all lone pairs and nonzero formal charges. You need only draw one Lewis structure for each molecule, even if there are multiple possible resonance structures.

b. Diazirinone decomposes in the gas phase over the course of several days at room temperature to give carbon monoxide and nitrogen gas. Based on the given BDEs, calculate $\Delta H^\circ$ for this decomposition reaction.

c. The actual $\Delta H^\circ$ for the decomposition of diazirinone is $-347\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Comment on any discrepancy you find between this value and the value you determined in part b. Be sure your comment addresses the direction of deviation of the two values.

d. Will $\Delta G^\circ$ for decomposition at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ be algebraically greater than, less than, or equal to $\Delta H^\circ$ for decomposition? Briefly justify your answer.

e. There is an isomer of diazirinone that has a chain structure with the connectivity $\ce{NCNO}$. Draw a Lewis structure for this molecule and clearly describe or sketch its geometry.

f. Would you expect acyclic $\ce{NCNO}$ to be more or less stable than diazirinone? Clearly justify your prediction.

Oxygen has two stable allotropes, $\ce{O2}$ (dioxygen) and $\ce{O3}$ (ozone).

a. Explain why $\ce{O2}$ has a higher normal boiling point than either $\ce{N2}$ or $\ce{F2}$.

d. Explain why $\ce{O2}$ does not absorb light in the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum but $\ce{O3}$ does.

e. Dioxygen can be oxidized to form dioxygenyl cation ($\ce{O2+}$) or reduced to form superoxide ion ($\ce{O2-}$) or peroxide ion ($\ce{O2^{2-}}$), while ozone can be reduced to form ozonide ion ($\ce{O3-}$). Fill in the table below by assigning the correct distances to the six species, and briefly justify your assignments. (You may consider $127$ and $128\,\mathrm{pm}$ as essentially the same in this problem.)

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Species} & \text{O--O distance, pm} & \text{Species} & \text{O--O distance, pm} \\
\hline
\ce{O2} & & & \\
\hline
\ce{O2+} & & \ce{O3} & \\
\hline
\ce{O2-} & & \ce{O3-} & \\
\hline
\ce{O2^{2-}} & & & \\

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Bond} & \textbf{BDE}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) \\
\hline
\ce{C#C} & 839 \\
\hline
\ce{C-H} & 412 \\
\hline
\ce{O=O} & 498 \\
\hline
\ce{C=O} & 741 \\
\hline
\ce{O-H} & 463 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

$$\ce{C2H2(g) + 2.5 O2(g) -> 2 CO2(g) + H2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{expt}} = -1256\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$$

(A) The tabulated $\ce{C-H}$ BDE does not account for the unusual strength of the bond formed to the $\textit{sp}$-hybridized carbon in $\ce{C2H2}$.
(B) The tabulated $\ce{O=O}$ BDE does not account for the unusual weakness of the bond in dioxygen due to its paramagnetism.
(C) The tabulated $\ce{C=O}$ BDE does not account for the stabilization due to electronic delocalization in carbon dioxide.

\ce{CH3I(aq) + OH^-(aq) -> CH3OH(aq) + I^-(aq)} & \qquad \mathrm{Rate} = k_2[\ce{CH3I}][\ce{OH^-}]
\end{array}$$

After $1.50\,\mathrm{h}$ at $89.9\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the concentration of iodide in this solution is measured to be $0.0311\,\mathrm{M}$. What is the value of $k_1$ at $89.9\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

b. What would the concentration of iodide be in this solution after $3.00\,\mathrm{h}$ at $89.9\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

The hydrolysis of iodomethane is studied in strongly buffered solutions as a function of pH. Under these conditions, the reaction is always found to be first order in iodomethane, with an observed first-order rate constant $k_{\mathrm{obs}}$ that varies with pH. The logarithms of $k_{\mathrm{obs}}$ (with $k_{\mathrm{obs}}$ measured in units of $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$) for the reaction studied at $333\,\mathrm{K}$ as a function of pH are shown with filled circles and a solid line on the graph below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/us-2026-3-4-fig1.png

c. What are the values of $k_1$ and $k_2$ for the reaction at $333\,\mathrm{K}$?

d. The analogous data for the reaction studied at $343\,\mathrm{K}$ are shown on the graph (filled squares, dashed line). Which has a larger activation energy, reaction 1 or reaction 2? Explain your reasoning.

Problem 7 (National Exam Part II).

Boron and hydrogen form a number of interesting compounds.

a. Give the electron configuration and the number of unpaired electrons in both the ground state of atomic $\mathrm{B}$ and its lowest-energy excited state.

b. Which requires more energy to excite, the ground state of atomic $\mathrm{B}$ to its lowest excited state or the ground state of atomic $\mathrm{H}$ to its lowest excited state? Justify your answer.

c. In the gas phase at low pressure, the binary compound $\ce{BH3}$ can be observed. Clearly describe or depict its geometry and explain its bonding.

d. At higher pressures or in condensed phases, $\ce{BH3}$ dimerizes to form diborane, $\ce{B2H6}$. Clearly describe or depict the geometry and explain the bonding in diborane.

Carboranes are neutral compounds with the formula $\ce{C2B10H12}$, where two of the boron atoms in $\ce{B12H12^{2-}}$ are replaced with carbon while retaining the same icosahedral structure. Problem 8 (National Exam Part II).

$(E)$-2-pentene reacts with hydrogen bromide to give three compounds, $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$. Compound $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with potassium hydroxide in dimethyl sulfoxide to give $(E)$-2-pentene and its $(Z)$ isomer as the only alkene products. In contrast, compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ react with $\ce{KOH}$ in DMSO to give not only $(E)$- and $(Z)$-2-pentene but also another alkene $\mathbf{D}$.

a. Draw structures for compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{D}$, clearly indicating stereochemistry if applicable.

b. What is the relationship (constitutional isomers, enantiomers, diastereomers, or not isomers) between compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$?

c. What is the relationship (constitutional isomers, enantiomers, diastereomers, or not isomers) between compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$?

d. $(E)$-2-pentene has a melting point of $-140\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a normal boiling point of $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while $(Z)$-2-pentene has a melting point of $-180\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a boiling point of $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Explain why the $(E)$ isomer has a significantly higher melting point, but essentially the same boiling point, as the $(Z)$ isomer.

e. No alkenes with the formula $\ce{C5H10}$ are chiral. Draw the structure of a chiral alkene with the formula $\ce{C6H12}$.
